title: DESIGN IT: the system-design interview
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 design-it row): the habits every DESIGN IT rubric rewards. Scope = the primary DESIGN IT sets on content/paths/sysdesign.json (after the S2 hand review); sources = the path sets whose key points teach the idea; siblings = sysdrills that exercise its maths. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Walk the same frame every time: requirements and numbers, entities and API, a high-level sketch, one deep dive, a pre-mortem, then the trade-offs you defend.
ideas.why: Without a frame you draw boxes before you know the load, run out of time before failure modes, and the interviewer never hears a decision.
ideas.prompt: You have 45 minutes and the prompt is 'design a booking service'. Ten minutes in you are already debating Kafka versus a database queue. What went wrong, and how do you recover the session?
ideas.answer: You skipped the opening steps. Stop and restate what users do and the non-functional asks (how many, how fast, how correct), put two or three numbers on the board, sketch entities and endpoints, then pick one deep dive. Queue choice belongs in the deep dive or the pre-mortem, once the load says you need one.

ideas.idea: State at least one envelope number out loud before you draw, and let it decide the design: whether one primary is enough, what the cache holds, where the peak lands.
ideas.why: Designs without numbers either over-build (sharding a few hundred writes a second) or under-build, and you cannot defend any box you drew.
ideas.prompt: An interviewer asks you to design a link shortener and immediately asks 'do you need to shard?'. What do you say first, and what would change your answer?
ideas.answer: First the envelope: writes and reads a second at average and peak, bytes per stored link, growth per year. If that lands at tens of writes and thousands of reads a second with a few hundred gigabytes over years, one primary plus a cache is enough. Sharding becomes the answer only when the numbers outgrow one machine.

ideas.idea: Name the consistency each piece of data needs, item by item: some reads may be seconds stale, others (uniqueness, money, stock) must be exact.
ideas.why: One global choice is wrong both ways: everything strongly consistent is slow and expensive, everything eventual oversells stock or hands out a taken name.
ideas.prompt: In a storefront you cache product pages, inventory counts and coupon codes. A colleague says 'eventual consistency everywhere, with a 60-second cache'. Go through the three and say where you agree.
ideas.answer: Product pages can be a minute stale; nobody is harmed. Inventory shown on a page can be stale, but the decrement at checkout must be exact against the database. Coupon redemption is a uniqueness rule: enforce it at write time in the store of record, never from a cached copy. Different data, different promises.

ideas.idea: Every write that can be retried, by a client, a queue or a webhook sender, must be safe to apply twice, with the dedupe decided where the write commits.
ideas.why: Retries are guaranteed in a distributed system; without a dedupe rule each timeout can become a double charge, a duplicate email or a second order.
ideas.prompt: A checkout endpoint times out at the client, which retries; the payment provider also re-sends its webhook. Walk through how one purchase ends up charged once, and where each guarantee lives.
ideas.answer: The client sends a key with the purchase; the server records that key together with the outcome when the order commits, so a retry gets the stored result instead of a second charge. Webhook events are recorded by their event id before acting, so a re-sent event is a no-op. Both checks live in the database transaction, not in memory.

ideas.idea: For each dependency, say what the system does when it is slow or down: fail open, fail closed, degrade, or queue, and why that is the right side.
ideas.why: Unplanned dependencies turn one outage into a total outage, and slow calls with no limits exhaust the threads and connections everything else needs.
ideas.prompt: Your API's rate limiter keeps its counters in Redis, and checkout calls a payment provider. Redis goes down, and the provider gets slow. What should the API do in each case?
ideas.answer: Decide per dependency. A limiter that rejects everything when its store is gone turns a cache outage into a full outage, so most tiers fail open, with a local fallback limit where abuse matters. The slow provider gets a timeout and its own concurrency limit, called outside the database transaction, so it cannot hold connections everyone needs.

ideas.idea: Look for the one key or row that takes a disproportionate share of traffic or writes, and say how the design survives it.
ideas.why: Averages hide hot spots: a viral item or a popular event's stock row saturates one shard or one lock while the fleet looks idle.
ideas.prompt: Concert tickets go on sale and 50,000 people try to buy from the same event in the first minute. Your design has a sharded cache and an events table. Where does it break first?
ideas.answer: On the single event: its cache key lands on one node and its stock row is updated by everyone, so writes serialize on that row. Protect the key (replicas, request coalescing, jittered expiry) and accept the hot-row contention or split the stock into holds; say which one you choose and what it costs.

ideas.idea: A queue needs a bound with backpressure, a rule for messages that never succeed, and someone who owns the parked messages.
ideas.why: An unbounded queue only postpones the outage, and a message that always fails either blocks the line or is silently lost.
ideas.prompt: Your background job queue grows by a million jobs during a partner outage, and one malformed job fails on every attempt. What has to be in the design before this happens?
ideas.answer: A limit on how much can wait, with producers slowed or refused when it is reached, instead of a queue that grows until memory runs out. Failures classified: retry the transient ones with backoff, set aside the hopeless ones after a few attempts in a separate parked queue, with an owner, an alert and a way to replay them.

ideas.idea: Put tenant isolation into the data model and every query path, not into the UI: the tenant id is part of the keys, indexes and permission checks.
ideas.why: One query that forgets the tenant filter leaks another customer's data, and a check only in the frontend is no check at all.
ideas.prompt: A B2B app stores projects for many companies in one database. A new report endpoint is written in a hurry. What structural choices make it hard for that endpoint to leak another company's projects?
ideas.answer: Every tenant-owned row carries the tenant id and its indexes start with it, so scoped queries are also the fast ones. The request layer resolves which tenant the caller acts in, and the data layer applies that scope on every read, so an endpoint cannot simply forget it. Resource checks still run per object.

ideas.idea: Say what is measured and what wakes a human: a small set of user-facing signals with targets, alerts that fire once per real problem, not per check run.
ideas.why: Without it nobody notices the slow failure, or on-call is flooded by repeats until they mute the alert that matters.
ideas.prompt: Your support platform checks every 30 seconds whether tickets are close to breaching their response deadline. On a bad morning it sends the same escalation dozens of times. What is missing from the design?
ideas.answer: A record that this alert, for this window and threshold, was already sent, stored durably and set before sending, so a re-run or a restart does not repeat it. Beyond that: decide which user-facing signals have targets, page on those, and send everything else to a dashboard or a ticket.

ideas.idea: Every design change ships with a rollout plan: old and new versions run side by side, data is moved in paced steps, and each step can be undone.
ideas.why: A big-bang schema change or reindex either locks the live product or leaves a half-migrated state you cannot roll back.
ideas.prompt: You must rename a column that every request reads, and rebuild the search index from it, without downtime. The app runs several instances during a rolling deploy. Lay out the steps.
ideas.answer: Add the new column first and write both, backfill in small paced batches, switch reads once the backfill is verified, and only then stop writing the old one and drop it, each step its own deploy. Build the new index alongside the old one and flip readers when it has caught up, so you can flip back.

ideas.idea: A trade-off is complete only when it names what was given up and why that loss is acceptable here.
ideas.why: 'We chose X because it scales' is not a decision; without the cost the interviewer cannot tell judgement from a memorised answer.
ideas.prompt: You decided that checkout locks the stock row so the shop can never oversell. The interviewer asks 'so what did that cost you?'. Give a complete answer.
ideas.answer: Contention: on a popular item buyers queue on one row, so checkout gets slower and some see sold-out errors under load. That is accepted because overselling costs refunds and trust, which is worse than a slower sold-out. If the hot items grow, the next step is reserving stock in holds, at the cost of more moving parts.
